     2	\section{Making measurements projective}
     3	\label{sec:making-measurements-projective}
     4	
     5	A recurring theme in $\MIP^*$ research is that 
     6	projective measurements are significantly easier to manipulate
     7	than general POVM measurements.
     8	As just one example among many,
     9	when $A = \{A^x_a\}$ and $B = \{B^x_a\}$ are projective measurements,
    10	the ``$\approx_\delta$" and ``$\simeq_\delta$" distances are equivalent.
    11	In other words:
    12	\begin{equation*}
    13	A^x_a \ot I \simeq_{\delta} I \ot B^x_a
    14	\qquad
    15	\iff
    16	\qquad
    17	A^x_a \ot I \approx_{2\delta} I \ot B^x_a.
    18	\end{equation*}
    19	This is Fact~$4.13$ from~\cite{NW19}.
    20	On the other hand when~$A$ and~$B$
    21	are not projective,
    22	one can find examples of measurements
    23	where $A^x_a \ot I \approx_{\delta} I \ot B^x_a$
    24	for $\delta \rightarrow 0$
    25	but one can show $A^x_a \ot I \simeq_{\eps} I \ot B^x_a$
    26	only for $\eps \rightarrow 1$;
    27	this is Remark~$4.15$ from~\cite{NW19}.
    28	As a result, it is important to be able to convert
    29	POVM measurements to projective measurements
    30	whenever possible.
    31	
    32	In this section, we will survey two tools for doing so.
    33	The first of these is the textbook Naimark dilation theorem.
    34	In our setting, it states the following.
    35	
    36	\begin{theorem}[Naimark dilation]\label{thm:naimark}
    37	Let $\ket{\psi}$ be a state in $\calH_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \calH_{\mathrm{B}}$.
    38	Let $A = \{A^x_a\}$ be a sub-measurement acting on $\calH_{\mathrm{A}}$
    39	and $B=\{B^y_b\}$ be a sub-measurement acting on $\calH_{\mathrm{B}}$.
    40	Then there exists
    41	\begin{enumerate}
    42	\item Hilbert spaces $\calH_{\mathrm{A}_{\mathsf{aux}}}$ and $\calH_{\mathrm{B}_{\mathsf{aux}}}$,
    43	\item a state $\ket{\mathsf{aux}} \in \calH_{\mathrm{A}_{\mathsf{aux}}} \ot \calH_{\mathrm{B}_{\mathsf{aux}}}$,
    44	\item and two measurements  $\widehat{A} = \{\widehat{A}^x_a\}$ and $\widehat{B}=\{\widehat{B}^y_b\}$
    45	acting on $\calH_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \calH_{\mathrm{A}_{\mathsf{aux}}}$
    46	and $\calH_{\mathrm{B}} \ot \calH_{\mathrm{B}_{\mathsf{aux}}}$,
    47	respectively,
    48	\end{enumerate}
    49	such that the following is true.
    50	If we write $\ket{\widehat{\psi}} = \ket{\psi} \otimes \ket{\mathsf{aux}}$,
    51	then for all $x,y, a, b$,
    52	 \begin{equation*}
    53	 \bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^y_b \ket{\psi}
    54	 = \bra{\widehat{\psi}} \widehat{A}^x_a \ot \widehat{B}^y_b \ket{\widehat{\psi}}.
    55	 \end{equation*}
    56	 In addition, $\ket{\mathsf{aux}}$ is a \emph{product state},
    57	 meaning that we can write it as
    58	 \begin{equation*}
    59	 \ket{\mathsf{aux}}= \ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{A}}} \ot \ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{B}}},
    60	 \end{equation*}
    61	for $\ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{A}}}$ in $\calH_{\mathrm{A}_{\mathsf{aux}}}$
    62	and $\ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{B}}}$ in $\calH_{\mathrm{B}_{\mathsf{aux}}}$.
    63	\end{theorem}
    64	The second of these is the ``orthogonalization lemma" from~\cite{KV11}.
    65	In the setting of symmetric strategies, it states the following.
    66	
    67	\begin{theorem}[Orthogonalization lemma]\label{thm:orthonormalization}
    68	Let $\ket{\psi}$ be a permutation-invariant state,
    69	and let $A = \{A_a\}$ be a sub-measurement with strong self-consistency
    70	\begin{equation*}
    71	\sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes A_a \ket{\psi} \geq \sum_a \bra{\psi} A_a \otimes I \ket{\psi} -\zeta.
    72	\end{equation*}
    73	Then there exists a projective sub-measurement $P = \{P_a\}$ such that
    74	\begin{equation*}
    75	A_a \otimes I \approx_{100 \zeta^{1/4}} P_a \otimes I.
    76	\end{equation*}
    77	\end{theorem}
    78	
    79	These two results serve largely the same purpose,
    80	and for our applications it will typically suffice to use either one.
    81	That said, there are tradeoffs when choosing to use one or the other.
    82	Naimark dilation is convenient because it can be applied to any family of sub-measurements
    83	and it preserves measurement outcome probabilities exactly.
    84	On the other hand, it requires swapping out the state $\ket{\psi}$ and measurements~$A$ and~$B$
    85	for $\ket{\widehat{\psi}}$ and $\widehat{A}$ and $\widehat{B}$, respectively,
    86	which can be notationally cumbersome.
    87	Most works opt to skip adding the hats,
    88	and instead say something to the effect of ``using Naimark, we can assume that~$A$ and~$B$ are projective."
    89	However, there is subtlety in doing so,
    90	which is that Naimark dilation does not necessarily preserve ``$\approx_{\delta}$" statements;
    91	in other words, $A^x_a \ot I \approx_{\delta} I \ot B^x_a$
    92	does not necessarily imply $\widehat{A}^x_a \ot I \approx_{\delta} I \ot \widehat{B}^x_a$.
    93	(As an example, \Cref{ex:easy-but-long} below
    94	provides a case in which $A^x_a \ot I \approx_{0} I \ot B^x_a$,
    95	but $\widehat{A}^x_a \ot I \approx_{\delta} I \ot \widehat{B}^x_a$ only holds for $\delta \geq 1$.)
    96	This can lead to trouble if the same notation is used for~$A, B$ and $\widehat{A}, \widehat{B}$,
    97	as ``$\approx_{\delta}$" statements derived before applying Naimark might not necessarily hold after applying Naimark.
    98	(That said, as pointed out at the end of Section~$4.4$ of~\cite{NW19},
    99	``$\approx_{\delta}$" statements are often derived as a consequence of ``$\simeq_{\delta}$" statements.
   100	And as Naimark preserves ``$\simeq_{\delta}$" statements,
   101	one could use them to simply rederive any ``$\approx_{\delta}$" statements post-Naimark.)
   102	
   103	The downsides of using the orthogonalization lemma
   104	are that it can only be applied to measurements which are strongly self-consistent
   105	and it introduces additional error.
   106	As we will see below, its proof is significantly more complicated than Naimark dilation.
   107	On the plus side, it has none of the notational baggage that Naimark brings,
   108	and so it is more concrete to use.
   109	In addition, it can lead to stronger results,
   110	as it does not require introducing an auxiliary state $\ket{\mathsf{aux}}$.
   111	
   112	In this work, we will opt to use the orthogonalization lemma rather than Naimark dilation.
   113	However, we will include proofs of both for completeness.
   114	We will prove \Cref{thm:naimark} in \Cref{sec:naimark}
   115	and then \Cref{thm:orthonormalization} in \Cref{sec:orthogonalization}.
   116	
   117	\subsection{Naimark dilation}\label{sec:naimark}
   118	
   119	To prove \Cref{thm:naimark}, we will first need the following lemma.
   120	
   121	\begin{lemma}
   122	  \label{lem:naimark-helper}
   123	  Let $A = \{A_{a}\}$ be a sub-measurement with $k$ distinct outcomes $a \in \calA$, and let $\ket{\mathsf{aux}} \in \C^{k+1}$ be any state. Then there exists a projective sub-measurement $\widehat{A} = \{\widehat{A}_{a}\}$ such that
   124	  for each outcome~$a$,
   125	  \[ (I \ot \bra{\mathsf{aux}} ) \cdot \widehat{A}_{a} \cdot (I \ot \ket{\mathsf{aux}}) =
   126	    A_{a}. \]
   127	\end{lemma}
   128	\begin{proof}
   129	We will consider an orthonormal basis for $\C^{k+1}$
   130	consisting of a vector $\ket{a}$ for each $a \in \calA$ and the vector $\ket{\bot}$.
   131	Let~$U$ be any unitary such that for each vector $\ket{\psi} \in \C^d$,
   132	\begin{align*}
   133	U \cdot (\ket{\psi} \ot \ket{\mathsf{aux}})
   134	&= \sum_{a \in \calA} ((A_{a})^{1/2} \ket{\psi}) \ot \ket{a} + ((1 - A)^{1/2}\ket{\psi}) \ot \ket{\bot}\\
   135	&= \Big(\sum_{a \in \calA} (A_{a})^{1/2} \ot \ket{a} + (1 - A)^{1/2} \ot \ket{\bot}\Big)
   136			\cdot \ket{\psi}.
   137	\end{align*}
   138	This implies that
   139	\begin{equation*}
   140	U \cdot (I \ot \ket{\mathsf{aux}})
   141	= \sum_{a \in \calA} (A_{a})^{1/2} \ot \ket{a} + (1 - A)^{1/2} \ot \ket{\bot}.
   142	\end{equation*}
   143	Hence, for any $a \in \calA$,
   144	\begin{equation*}
   145	(I \ot \bra{a}) \cdot U \cdot (I \ot \ket{\mathsf{aux}})
   146	= (I \ot \bra{a}) \cdot \Big(\sum_{a \in \calA} (A_{a})^{1/2} \ot \ket{a} + (1 - A)^{1/2} \ot \ket{\bot}\Big)
   147	= (A_a)^{1/2}.
   148	\end{equation*}
   149	  Then the desired projective sub-measurement is
   150	  \[ \widehat{A}_a = U^{\dagger} \cdot (I \ot \ket{a} \bra{a}) \cdot U. \]
   151	  This is because
   152	\begin{align*}
   153	 (I \ot \bra{\mathsf{aux}} ) \cdot \widehat{A}_{a} \cdot (I \ot \ket{\mathsf{aux}})
   154	&=(I \ot \bra{\mathsf{aux}} ) \cdot (U^{\dagger} \cdot (I \ot \ket{a} \bra{a}) \cdot U) \cdot (I \ot \ket{\mathsf{aux}})\\

   156	&= (A_a)^{1/2} \cdot (A_a)^{1/2} = A_a.

   158	This completes the proof.

   835	Now we introduce our main tool for studying~$X$, which is via its singular value decomposition.

   837	\begin{definition}[SVD of~$X$]
   838	Let $X = U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger$ be the singular value decomposition (SVD) of~$X$.
   839	Because~$X$ is an $m \times d$ matrix,
   840	the definition of the SVD states that
   841	$U$ is an $m \times m$ unitary matrix,
   842	$V$ is a $d \times d$ unitary matrix,
   843	and $\Sigma_{m\times d}$ is an $m \times d$ diagonal matrix
   844	with nonnegative real numbers on its diagonal.
   845	\end{definition}
   846	
   847	\begin{notation}
   848	For positive integers $h$ and~$w$,
   849	we will write $I_{h \times w}$ for the $h \times w$ matrix with $1$'s on its diagonal and $0$'s everywhere else.
   850	
   851	For integers $h, w \geq m$, we also write $\Sigma_{h \times w}$
   852	for the $h \times w$ diagonal matrix whose diagonal agrees with $\Sigma_{m \times d}$'s;
   853	namely, $(\Sigma_{h \times w})_{i, i} = (\Sigma_{m \times d})_{i,i}$ for all $1 \leq i \leq m$
   854	and $(\Sigma_{h \times w})_{i, i} = 0$ for all $i > m$.
   855	We note that because $\Sigma_{m \times d}$ is a real-valued diagonal matrix,
   856	$(\Sigma_{h \times w})^\dagger = \Sigma_{w \times h}$.
   857	\end{notation}
   858	
   859	With this definition,
   860	we can give a helpful expression for the square of~$X$.
   861	
   862	\begin{lemma}[$X$ squared]\label{lem:X-squared}
   863	\begin{equation*}
   864	X \cdot X^\dagger = U  \cdot (\Sigma_{m \times m})^2 \cdot U^\dagger,
   865	\quad
   866	\text{and}
   867	\quad
   868	X^\dagger \cdot X = Q = V \cdot (\Sigma_{d \times d})^2 \cdot V^\dagger.
   869	\end{equation*}
   870	\end{lemma}
   871	\begin{proof}
   872	First,
   873	\begin{align*}
   874	X \cdot X^\dagger
   875	&= (U  \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger) \cdot (U  \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger\\
   876	&= U  \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \cdot V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger\\
   877	&= U  \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot I_{d \times d} \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$V$ is a $d \times d$ unitary}\\
   878	&= U  \cdot (\Sigma_{m \times m})^2 \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$m \leq d$}.
   879	\end{align*}
   880	Second,
   881	\begin{align*}
   882	X^\dagger \cdot X
   883	& = \sum_a X^\dagger \cdot T_a X  \tag{because~$T$ is a measurement}\\
   884	&= \sum_a Q_a \tag{by \Cref{lem:qa-restated}}\\
   885	&= Q.
   886	\end{align*}
   887	In addition, we can rewrite $X^\dagger \cdot X$ as
   888	\begin{align*}
   889	X^\dagger \cdot X
   890	&= (U  \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger \cdot (U  \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)\\
   891	&= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \cdot U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger\\
   892	&= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \tag{because~$U$ is an $m \times m$ unitary}\\
   893	&= V \cdot (\Sigma_{d \times d})^2 \cdot V^\dagger.
   894	\end{align*}
   895	This completes the proof.
   896	\end{proof}

   898	The following lemma relates an expression in the $X_a$'s
   899	with an expression in the~$Q_a$'s that appeared previously in \Cref{lem:q-almost-projective}.
   900	
   901	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:X-expression-to-Q-expression}
   902	For each~$a$,
   903	\begin{equation*}
   904	X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot X_a
   905	= Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - Q_a.
   906	\end{equation*}
   907	\end{lemma}
   908	\begin{proof}
   909	Using~\Cref{lem:X-squared} and~\Cref{lem:qa-restated},
   910	\begin{equation*}
   911	X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger \cdot X \cdot X^\dagger) \cdot X_a
   912	= X_a^\dagger \cdot X \cdot Q \cdot X^\dagger \cdot X_a
   913	= Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a.
   914	\end{equation*}
   915	Similarly, because $Q_a$ is projective,
   916	\begin{equation*}
   917	X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger) \cdot X_a
   918	= (X_a^\dagger \cdot X) \cdot (X^\dagger \cdot X_a)
   919	= Q_a \cdot Q_a
   920	= Q_a.
   921	\end{equation*}
   922	Finally,
   923	\begin{equation*}
   924	X_a^\dagger \cdot (I_{m \times m}) \cdot X_a
   925	= X_a^\dagger \cdot X_a = Q_a.
   926	\end{equation*}
   927	Putting these together,
   928	\begin{align*}
   929	&X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot X_a\\
   930	 =~& X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger \cdot X \cdot X^\dagger  - 2 \cdot X\cdot X^\dagger + I_{m \times m}) \cdot X_a\\
   931	    =~& Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a  - 2 \cdot Q_a  + Q_a\\
   932	    =~& Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a  -  Q_a.
   933	\end{align*}
   934	This completes the proof.
   935	\end{proof}

   937	Now we are ready to state the projective sub-measurement~$P$
   938	which should approximate~$A$.
   939	Before doing so, we give some intuition for the construction.
   940	
   941	\begin{remark}
   942	Suppose that the $Q_a$'s actually formed a projective measurement.
   943	This would imply that the vectors $\ket{v_{a, i}}$, over all $a$ and $1 \leq i \leq m_a$ form an orthonormal set.
   944	Then the SVD would actually have already been provided in \Cref{eq:looks-like-singular-value-decomposition};
   945	for each $a$ and $1 \leq i \leq m_a$,
   946	the corresponding singular value would be~$1$ and the corresponding left- and right-singular vectors would be $\ket{a, i}$ and $\ket{v_{a, i}}$, respectively.
   947	In particular, we would have $\Sigma = I_{m \times d}$ and $X = U \cdot I_{m \times d}\cdot V^\dagger$.
   948	\end{remark}
   949	
   950	In reality, we don't know that $\Sigma = I_{m \times d}$.
   951	However, we will construct~$P = \{P_a\}$ as if it were.
   952	This motivates the following definition.
   953	
   954	\begin{definition}[Definition of~$P$]
   955	Define the matrix 
   956	\begin{equation*}
   957	\widehat{X} = U  \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger.
   958	\end{equation*}
   959	In addition, for each $a$, define the matrices
   960	\begin{equation*}
   961	\widehat{X}_a  = T_a \cdot \widehat{X},
   962	\quad P_a  = \widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}_a.
   963	\end{equation*}
   964	\end{definition}
   965	
   966	We now give analogues of \Cref{lem:qa-restated,lem:X-squared} for the~$P$ matrices.
   967	
   968	\begin{lemma}[$P_a$ restated]\label{lem:pa-restated}
   969	For each~$a$,
   970	\begin{equation*}
   971	P_a = \widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X} = \widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}.
   972	\end{equation*}
   973	\end{lemma}
   974	\begin{proof}
   975	This follows from the definition of $\widehat{X}^\dagger_a$ and the fact that $T$ is a projective measurement:
   976	\begin{equation*}
   977	P_a
   978	= \widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}_a
   979	= (\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a) \cdot (T_a  \cdot \widehat{X})
   980	= \widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X} = \widehat{X}_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}.\qedhere
   981	\end{equation*}
   982	\end{proof}
   983	
   984	\begin{lemma}[$\widehat{X}$ squared]\label{lem:X-hat-squared}
   985	\begin{equation*}
   986	\widehat{X} \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger = I_{m \times m}.
   987	\end{equation*}
   988	\end{lemma}
   989	\begin{proof}
   990	First,
   991	\begin{align*}
   992	\widehat{X} \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger
   993	&= (U  \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger) \cdot (U  \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger\\
   994	&= U  \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \cdot V \cdot I_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger\\
   995	&= U  \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot I_{d \times d} \cdot I_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$V$ is a $d \times d$ unitary}\\
   996	&= U  \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$m \leq d$}\\
   997	&= I_{m \times m},
   998	\end{align*}
   999	where the last step uses the fact that~$U$ is an $m \times m$ unitary.
  1000	
  1001	\end{proof}
  1002	
  1003	Finally, we show two lemmas on quantities involving both $X$ and~$\widehat{X}$.
  1004	
  1005	\begin{lemma}[$X$ times $\widehat{X}$]\label{lem:X-times-X-hat}
  1006	\begin{equation*}
  1007	X \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger = U  \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m} \cdot U^\dagger,
  1008	\quad
  1009	\text{and}
  1010	\quad
  1011	X^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} = \sqrt{Q}.
  1012	\end{equation*}
  1013	\end{lemma}
  1014	\begin{proof}
  1015	First,
  1016	\begin{align*}
  1017	X \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger
  1018	&= (U  \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger) \cdot (U  \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger\\
  1019	&= U  \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \cdot V \cdot I_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger\\
  1020	&= U  \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot I_{d \times d} \cdot I_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$V$ is a $d \times d$ unitary}\\
  1021	&= U  \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \tag{because~$m \leq d$}.
  1022	\end{align*}
  1023	Second,
  1024	\begin{align*}
  1025	X^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X}
  1026	&= (U  \cdot \Sigma_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)^\dagger \cdot (U  \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger)\\
  1027	&= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot U^\dagger \cdot U \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger\\
  1028	&= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times m} \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot I_{m \times d} \cdot V^\dagger \tag{because~$U$ is an $m \times m$ unitary}\\
  1029	&= V \cdot \Sigma_{d \times d} \cdot V^\dagger\\
  1030	&= \sqrt{V \cdot (\Sigma_{d \times d})^2 \cdot V^\dagger}\\
  1031	&= \sqrt{Q}. \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-squared}}
  1032	\end{align*}
  1033	This completes the proof.
  1034	\end{proof}
  1035	
  1036	\begin{lemma}[Squared difference]\label{lem:squared-difference}
  1037	\begin{equation*}
  1038	(X - \widehat{X}) \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger \leq (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2.
  1039	\end{equation*}
  1040	\end{lemma}
  1041	\begin{proof}
  1042	By~\Cref{lem:X-squared,lem:X-hat-squared,lem:X-times-X-hat},
  1043	\begin{align*}
  1044	(X - \widehat{X}) \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger
  1045	& = X \cdot X^\dagger  - X\cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger - \widehat{X} \cdot X^\dagger + \widehat{X} \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger\\
  1046	& = U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m}^2 \cdot U^\dagger  - 2 \cdot U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m} \cdot U^\dagger+ I_{m \times m}\\
  1047	& = U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m}^2   - 2 \cdot  \Sigma_{m \times m} +  I_{m \times m} \right) \cdot U^\dagger\\
  1048	& = U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m}  -  I_{m \times m}\right)^2 \cdot U^\dagger.
  1049	\end{align*}
  1050	Because $\Sigma_{m \times m}$ and $I_{m \times m}$ are commuting,
  1051	\begin{equation*}
  1052	(\Sigma_{m \times m} - I_{m \times m})^2
  1053	\leq (\Sigma_{m \times m} + I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot (\Sigma_{m \times m} - I_{m \times m})^2
  1054	= (\Sigma_{m\times m}^2 - I_{m \times m})^2.
  1055	\end{equation*}
  1056	As a result,
  1057	\begin{align*}
  1058	U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m}  -  I_{m \times m}\right)^2 \cdot U^\dagger
  1059	& \leq U \cdot \left(\Sigma_{m \times m}^2 -  I_{m \times m}\right)^2 \cdot U^\dagger\\
  1060	& = \left(U \cdot \Sigma_{m \times m}^2 \cdot U^\dagger - I_{m \times m} \right)^2\\
  1061	&= (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2. \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-squared}}
  1062	\end{align*}
  1063	This completes the proof.
  1064	\end{proof}
  1065	
  1066	The first property we need of~$P$ is that it is a projective sub-measurement.
  1067	This is shown in the following lemma.
  1068	
  1069	\begin{lemma}[Projectivity of~$P$]\label{lem:P-projectivity}
  1070	$P = \{P_a\}$ forms a projective sub-measurement.
  1071	\end{lemma}
  1072	\begin{proof}
  1073	Let $a, b$ be (possibly distinct) outcomes.
  1074	Then
  1075	\begin{align*}
  1076	P_a \cdot P_b
  1077	&= (\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X})
  1078		\cdot (\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_b \cdot \widehat{X}) \tag{by \Cref{lem:pa-restated}}\\
  1079	&= (\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot T_b \cdot \widehat{X}) \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-hat-squared}}\\
  1080	&= (\widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a  \cdot \widehat{X}) \cdot \bone[a = b] \tag{because~$T$ is a projective measurement}\\
  1081	&= P_a  \cdot \bone[a=b]. \tag{by \Cref{lem:pa-restated}}
  1082	\end{align*}
  1083	This completes the proof.
  1084	\end{proof}
  1085	
  1086	The second property we need of~$P$ is that it is close to~$A$.
  1087	We will first show that it is close to~$Q$.
  1088	
  1089	\begin{lemma}[$P$ is close to~$Q$]\label{lem:P-Q-approx}
  1090	\begin{equation*}
  1091	Q_a \otimes I \approx_{30\zeta^{1/4}} P_a \otimes I.
  1092	\end{equation*}
  1093	\end{lemma}
  1094	\begin{proof}
  1095	Our goal is to upper-bound the quantity
  1096	\begin{align}
  1097	&\sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a - P_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\
  1098	=~& \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} + \sum_a \bra{\psi} (P_a)^2 \otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}
  1099		- \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\nonumber\\
  1100	=~& \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi} +  \bra{\psi} P\otimes I \ket{\psi} - \sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}
  1101		- \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi},\label{eq:P-Q-thing-to-bound}
  1102	\end{align}
  1103	where the last step uses the projectivity of~$Q$ and~$P$.
  1104	We bound the four terms in \Cref{eq:P-Q-thing-to-bound} separately.
  1105	First, by \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum},
  1106	\begin{equation*}
  1107	 \bra{\psi} Q \otimes I \ket{\psi}
  1108	 \leq (1+2\sqrt{\zeta}) \cdot \bra{\psi} I \otimes I \ket{\psi} \leq 1+2\sqrt{\zeta}.
  1109	\end{equation*}
  1110	Second, because~$P$ is a sub-measurement,
  1111	\begin{equation*}
  1112	\bra{\psi} P \ot I\ket{\psi} \leq 1.
  1113	\end{equation*}
  1114	
  1115	The third term and fourth terms are significantly more complicated to bound.
  1116	As they are complex conjugates of each other, we can write their sum as
  1117	\begin{equation}\label{eq:complex-conjugates}
  1118	\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}
  1119		+ \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}
  1120	= 2 \cdot \mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Big).
  1121	\end{equation}
  1122	We now focus on the expression on the right-hand side of \Cref{eq:complex-conjugates}.
  1123	To begin, we use \Cref{lem:qa-restated} to rewrite it as
  1124	\begin{equation*}
  1125	\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}
  1126	= \sum_a \bra{\psi} ((X_a^\dagger \cdot X) \cdot P_a)  \otimes I \ket{\psi}.
  1127	\end{equation*}
  1128	The main step will be to show that we can exchange the second $X$ for an $\widehat{X}$, i.e.
  1129	\begin{equation}\label{eq:add-a-hat}
  1130	\sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot X \cdot P_a) \otimes I \ket{\psi}
  1131	\approx_{2\zeta^{1/4}} \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a)  \otimes I \ket{\psi}.
  1132	\end{equation}
  1133	To show this, we bound the magnitude of the difference.
  1134	\begin{multline*}
  1135	\Big|\sum_a \bra{\psi} ((X_a^\dagger \cdot (X - \widehat{X})) \ot I) \cdot(P_a \ot I) \ket{\psi}\Big|\\
  1136	\leq \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi}(X_a^\dagger \cdot (X - \widehat{X})  \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger \cdot X_a) \ot I \ket{\psi}}\cdot \sqrt{\sum_a \bra{\psi} (P_a)^2 \ot I \ket{\psi}}.
  1137	\end{multline*}
  1138	The expression inside the first square root is
  1139	\begin{align*}
  1140	& \sum_a \bra{\psi}(X_a^\dagger \cdot (X - \widehat{X})  \cdot (X - \widehat{X})^\dagger \cdot X_a) \ot I \ket{\psi}\\
  1141	\leq~&  \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot (X \cdot X^\dagger - I_{m \times m})^2 \cdot X_a) \ot I \ket{\psi}\tag{by \Cref{lem:squared-difference}}\\
  1142	=~&  \sum_a \bra{\psi} (Q_a \cdot Q \cdot Q_a - Q_a)  \ot I \ket{\psi}\tag{by \Cref{lem:X-expression-to-Q-expression}}\\
  1143	\leq~& 4\sqrt{\zeta} \cdot \bra{\psi} I \ot I \ket{\psi} \tag{by~\Cref{lem:q-almost-projective}}\\
  1144	=~& 4\sqrt{\zeta}.
  1145	\end{align*}
  1146	The expression inside the second square root is at most~$1$ because~$P$ is a sub-measurement.
  1147	Next, we claim that the \Cref{eq:add-a-hat} is in fact a real-valued expression.
  1148	To see this,
  1149	\begin{align*}
  1150	\eqref{eq:add-a-hat}
  1151	& = \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a)  \otimes I \ket{\psi}\\
  1152	&= \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot \widehat{X}^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) \ot I \ket{\psi}
  1153				\tag{by \Cref{lem:xa-t,lem:pa-restated}}\\
  1154	&= \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot T_a \cdot I_{m \times m} \cdot T_a \cdot \widehat{X}) \ot I \ket{\psi} \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-hat-squared}}\\
  1155	&= \sum_a \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger \cdot T_a  \cdot \widehat{X}) \ot I \ket{\psi}\\
  1156	&=  \bra{\psi} (X^\dagger  \cdot \widehat{X}) \ot I \ket{\psi} \tag{because~$T$ is a measurement}\\
  1157	&=  \bra{\psi} \sqrt{Q} \ot I \ket{\psi} \tag{by \Cref{lem:X-times-X-hat}},
  1158	\end{align*}
  1159	which is real-valued because~$Q$ is positive semidefinite.
  1160	As a result, we have
  1161	\begin{align*}
  1162	\mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Big)
  1163	& \geq \mathfrak{R}\Big(\sum_a \bra{\psi} (X_a^\dagger \cdot \widehat{X} \cdot P_a)  \otimes I \ket{\psi}\Big) - 2\zeta^{1/4} \tag{by \Cref{eq:add-a-hat}}\\
  1164	& = \bra{\psi} \sqrt{Q} \ot I \ket{\psi}- 2\zeta^{1/4}\\
  1165	& \geq (1 - 12 \zeta^{1/4}) - 2\zeta^{1/4}. \tag{by \Cref{lem:sqrt-Q-completeness}}
  1166	\end{align*}
  1167	In total, \Cref{eq:complex-conjugates} shows that
  1168	\begin{equation*}
  1169	\sum_a \bra{\psi} Q_a P_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}
  1170		+ \sum_a \bra{\psi} P_a Q_a \otimes I \ket{\psi}
  1171	\geq 2 \cdot(1 - 14\zeta^{1/4}).
  1172	\end{equation*}
  1173	Putting everything together, we conclude that
  1174	\begin{equation*}
  1175	\eqref{eq:P-Q-thing-to-bound}
  1176	\leq (1 + 2\sqrt{\zeta}) + 1 - 2\cdot (1-14\zeta^{1/4}) 
  1177	= 2\sqrt{\zeta} + 28 \zeta^{1/4}
  1178	\leq 30 \zeta^{1/4}.
  1179	\end{equation*}
  1180	This completes the proof.
  1181	\end{proof}
  1182	
  1183	Finally, we have that
  1184	\begin{align*}
  1185	A_a \ot I
  1186	&\approx_{12 \sqrt{\zeta}} Q_a \ot I \tag{by \Cref{lem:projective-low-rank-sum}}\\
  1187	&\approx_{30 \zeta^{1/4}} P_a \ot I. \tag{by \Cref{lem:P-Q-approx}}
  1188	\end{align*}
  1189	Hence, \Cref{prop:triangle-inequality-for-approx_delta} implies that
  1190	\begin{equation*}
  1191	A_a \ot I \approx_{84 \zeta^{1/4}} P_a \ot I.
  1192	\end{equation*}
  1193	This completes the proof.
  1194	\end{proof}

574:## Reviewer checklist
- **Genuine external citations.** `PolishchukSpielmanClassicalSoundnessStatement`
  cites the Polishchuk–Spielman theorem; we don't plan to formalize it.
- **Mathlib gaps we can't fill.** `hMatrixChernoff` in `chernoffBernoulliMatrix`
  is a Mathlib matrix-Chernoff-type statement; we flagged the gap upstream.
- **Tracked internal obligations.** A `*Statement` that has an open sub-issue
  and a named construction theorem target is trackable proof debt. It is still
  not an acceptable extra hypothesis on a source-labelled paper theorem.

### Unacceptable external smuggles

- A `*Statement` with no open tracking issue, no docstring explaining the
  mathematical gap, and no consumer-side comment flagging the smuggle.
- A `*Statement` whose body is the theorem's conclusion, wearing a different
  name (A1 in disguise).
- A `*Statement` used to close a lemma whose paper version does not require
  any such external assumption (silent strengthening of the Lean theorem
  relative to the paper's).

### How to spot it

Grep for these suffixes: `*Statement`, `*Witness`, `*Claim`,
`*Conclusion`, `*Output`, `*Input`, `*Hypothesis`, `*Requirement`,
`*Assumption`, `*Package` (that isn't a `*BridgePackage`). For each, ask:

- Is there a theorem anywhere that **constructs** a value of this type from the
  paper hypotheses?
- If not, is the absence explained in a docstring / tracking issue /
  `audits/` entry?
- Does the paper depend on an external theorem of this shape?

If any answer is "no", the structure is an unacceptable smuggle.

### Current status (audited 2026-05-08)

The May 2026 re-audit
([`audits/2026-05-08_statement-smuggle-reaudit.md`](../blob/main/audits/2026-05-08_statement-smuggle-reaudit.md))
classified 39 `*Statement` structures (102 declarations total across the
extended suffix sweep of `*Witness`/`*Conclusion`/`*Input`/etc.).

The live ledger is [#1379], replacing the now-closed [#449] (2026-05-01) and
[#451] (2026-04-30). Headline counts from the re-audit: 33 grounded, 2 tracked
smuggle, 2 external citation, 1 paper-faithful packaging, 1 dead. Without a live
ledger, **5 `*Statement` structures landed between 2026-04-18 and 2026-05-08
without a tracker entry** — the gap this policy fixes.

The Section 5 spectral-truncation chain is now an example of the preferred
migration: the old `SpectralTruncationInput` abbreviation has been removed, and
later arguments call direct constructors for `SpectralTruncationStatement`
instead of carrying an `Input` wrapper.

If you add a new `*Statement`-style structure to this codebase, include a
def-site docstring with its paper origin (per the "earn your place" policy in
[#1379]). If no construction theorem exists yet, file a sub-issue in [#1379]
and ship the source-faithful construction theorem with an explicit unfinished
proof obligation. Do not add the structure as a new source-theorem hypothesis
merely to keep downstream declarations compiling.

### Merge gate — new `*Statement` / `*Witness` / `*Input` structures

To prevent dead scaffolds from landing unnoticed (the 5-structure gap of
2026-04-18–2026-05-08), every PR that introduces a new `structure XStatement`,
`structure XWitness`, `structure XInput`, `abbrev XStatement`, or
`abbrev XInput` must satisfy **at least one** of these before merge:

1. **Has a construction theorem.** A theorem that constructs a value of this
   type from the appropriate paper hypotheses appears in the same PR or an
   already-merged ancestor. If the proof is not finished, the theorem must carry
   the explicit tracked proof obligation rather than moving the assertion into a
   paper-facing theorem's hypotheses.
2. **Has a consumer.** A theorem that takes a value of this type as a
   hypothesis appears in the same PR or an already-merged ancestor.
3. **Has a ledger entry.** A classification comment (G / E / T / P / D, per
   the verdict key in [#1379]) is posted on [#1379] as an issue comment, and
   the structure's def-site docstring links to that comment.

Structures that satisfy none of the above are dead on arrival and must not
merge.

### Related issues

- [#1379] — live `*Statement` ledger (replaces closed [#449] / [#451])
- [#449] — historical paper-wide gap tracker (closed 2026-05-01)
- [#451] — historical bridge-hypothesis tracker (closed 2026-04-30)
- [#278] — the original "derive `PermInvState` internally" discussion

---

## Reviewer checklist

Use this alongside the blocker
list in the lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference and the [`proof_frontier_review.md`](./proof_frontier_review.md)
checklist for structure fields. For any theorem or lemma that claims a paper
result, ask:

- [ ] **Hypothesis audit.** Does any hypothesis contain (up to `∃`/`∧`) the
      theorem's conclusion? If yes, that's A1 — reject or strengthen.
- [ ] **Definitional audit.** Is the proof `rfl` or a one-line `simp`? If
      yes, does the unfolded definition do the paper's math, or just match
      the shape of the conclusion? The latter is A2.
- [ ] **Domain audit.** Does the function have a fallback branch (`if
      eligible ... else default`)? If yes, does the theorem's signature
      require eligibility? If not, that's A3.
- [ ] **Witness audit.** Does the proof pick `x := default` for an
      existential named after a paper lemma? That's A4 unless the witness
      is genuinely unique-up-to-isomorphism.
- [ ] **Mathlib audit.** Is there a `private lemma` that duplicates a
      Mathlib fact? Run `exact?` / `apply?` / `#find` before accepting it
      (A5).
- [ ] **External-citation audit.** Does the proof consume a `*Statement` /
      `*Witness` / `*Package`? Is there a tracking issue that names its
      grounding plan (A6)?
- [ ] **Paper-faithfulness.** Does the Lean signature match the paper's
      statement, or does Lean sneak in extra hypotheses? Flag divergences
      as ⚠️S in [#1379].

A lemma that passes all of these is a proof. A lemma that fails one is
scaffolding, and should be labelled and tracked as such (don't tag with
`\leanok` until the gap is closed).

## CI prevention

Mechanical detection is possible for many of these patterns:

- **A1 (conclusion-shaped hypothesis).** Use
  `python3 scripts/audit_conclusion_shaped_hypotheses.py --ci` as the current
  report-only tripwire for the PR [#491] inline-existential mutation. It parses
  theorem/lemma headers and warns when an explicit existential hypothesis shares
  the conclusion's salient structure, while printing witness-adapter helpers
  separately. When [#438] lands (`\leanok` ↔ `sorryAx` drift), extend the same
  idea to all `\leanok`-tagged declarations: parse the hypothesis list; if any
  hypothesis's type (modulo `∃`/`∀`/`∧`) contains a prefix of the conclusion
  structure, warn.
- **A2 (definitional sleight).** Grep for `theorem <Name>.* := rfl` where
  `<Name>` has a blueprint `\lean{}` cross-reference. The only allowed cases
  are ones annotated with `@[paper_bookkeeping]` (proposed attribute) or in
  an allow-list.
- **A3 (zero-fallback).** Grep for identifier suffixes `fallback`, `or0`,
  `orDefault`, `placeholder`, `sentinel` in `Defs/*` files. Each should have
  a docstring citing the downstream eligibility precondition.
- **A4 (default witnesses).** Grep `:= default`, `refine ⟨default`, `exact
  ⟨default`, `Classical.arbitrary` inside proof bodies (not typeclass
  definitions). Cross-reference to [#1379]'s witness ledger.
- **A5 (Mathlib bypass).** No reliable CI check, but `audits/` reports
  catch it during per-chapter audits.
- **A6 (external smuggles).** Every new `structure *Statement` without a
  producing theorem should be required to carry a `/-- Grounded by: #NNN
  -/` docstring, enforced by a lint rule over `blueprint/`.

The scripts in `scripts/` (notably `scripts/blueprint_lean_sync.py` and
`scripts/blueprint_leanok_axioms.py`) are the natural home for extensions that
add these checks.

## See also

- the lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference — kernel-level blockers
  (`sorry`, `native_decide`, bare `axiom`, etc.); local addenda in
  [`project_conventions.md`](./project_conventions.md).
- [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](./CONTRIBUTING.md) — overall contributor workflow;
  review checklist section should link here.
- the lean-conventions `MATHLIB_pr-review` reference — detailed PR review guidelines.
- the lean-conventions `MATHLIB_naming` and `MATHLIB_style` references — Mathlib
  conventions; avoiding A5 (bypassing Mathlib) often starts with using
  Mathlib's names.
- [#1379] — live `*Statement` ledger (replaces [#449], [#451])
- [#449], [#451], [#477], [#493], [#494], [#495] — concrete trackers for
  the anti-patterns documented here.

 # Section 5 — Locality-preserving projectivization repair
 
 This file proves the locality-preserving repair route for the late Section 5
 `Q/X/XHat/P` argument.
 
 ## Scope
 
 The **spectral-truncation stage** (the first part of the proof of rounding
 to projectors) is already proved by
 `spectralTruncationStatement_of_sourceAlmostProjective` in
 `MakingMeasurementsProjective/SpectralTruncation/ProjectiveNonMeasurement.lean`,
 which is fully proved via
 `projectiveNonMeasurement_of_sourceAlmostProjective_full`. Proofs that
 require the spectral truncation statement should call that declaration directly.
 
 The main result recorded here:
 
 - **`leftLiftedProjectivizationRepair`** — paper origin
   `references/ldt-paper/orthonormalization.tex` lines 534–860 (rank
   reduction and the `Q`/`√Q` completeness setup) and 862–1194 (the
   `X`/`X̂`/`P` algebra producing the lifted projective sub-measurement,
   including the final triangle-inequality assembly).  The formal proof below
   follows that local `Q/X/XHat/P` route by passing to the left marginal state,
   constructing the local projective family there, and transporting the final
   estimate back to left lifts.
 
 The theorem proved here is the direct output of that route under a normalized
 bipartite state and the source almost-projective estimate for the left-lifted
 measurement. It is stated directly in terms of this estimate, rather than in
 terms of a separate repair-input assumption, and provides the unconditional
 repair step used by the orthonormalization theorem.

+private def diagBlock {ιA ιB : Type*}

 lemma matrix_eq_zero_of_rank_eq_zero {m n : Type*}
     [Finite m] [Fintype n] (A : Matrix m n ℂ) (hA : A.rank = 0) :
     A = 0 := by
   let _ : Fintype m := Fintype.ofFinite m
   classical
   have hrange : A.mulVecLin.range = ⊥ := by
     rw [Matrix.rank] at hA
     exact Submodule.finrank_eq_zero.mp hA
   ext i j
   have hv : A.mulVecLin (Pi.single j 1) ∈ A.mulVecLin.range := ⟨Pi.single j 1, rfl⟩
   have hv0 : A.mulVecLin (Pi.single j 1) = 0 := by
     simpa [hrange] using hv
   have hentry := congrArg (fun w => w i) hv0
   simpa [Matrix.mulVecLin_apply, Matrix.mulVec, dotProduct, Finset.sum_ite_eq,
     Pi.single_apply] using hentry

     {ιA ιB : Type*}
     [Fintype ιA] [DecidableEq ιA] [Fintype ιB] [DecidableEq ιB]
     [Fintype Outcome]
     {ψ : QuantumState (ιA × ιB)} {A : Measurement Outcome ιA}
     {R : OpFamily Outcome ιA}
     {P : ProjSubMeas Outcome ιA}
     {δ : Error}
     (hR : ∀ a : Outcome, R.outcome a = P.outcome a)
     (hclose :
       SDDOpRel ψ (uniformDistribution Unit)
         (fun _ => OpFamily.leftPlacedOpFamily (ιB := ιB) (A.toSubMeas : OpFamily Outcome ιA))
         (fun _ => OpFamily.leftPlacedOpFamily (ιB := ιB) R)

       (constSubMeasFamily (leftPlacedSubMeas (ιB := ιB) A.toSubMeas))
       (constSubMeasFamily (leftPlacedSubMeas (ιB := ιB) P.toSubMeas))
       δ := by

   have herror :
       sddError ψ (uniformDistribution Unit)

+\begin{definition}[Formalization support for marginal reduction]
+	\label{def:left-marginal-state}
+	\lean{MIPStarRE.LDT.MakingMeasurementsProjective.leftMarginalState}
+	\leanok
+	Let $\rho$ be the density operator of a state on
+	$\hilb_{\mathsf A}\ot\hilb_{\mathsf B}$, where $\hilb_{\mathsf B}$ is nonzero
+	and both spaces are finite dimensional. Relative to an orthonormal basis $\{e_b\}$ of
+	$\hilb_{\mathsf B}$, define its normalized left marginal $\rho_{\mathsf A}$ by
+	\[
+		\bra{i}\rho_{\mathsf A}\ket{j}
+		= \frac{1}{\dim \hilb_{\mathsf B}}\sum_b
+		\bra{i,e_b}\rho\ket{j,e_b}.
+	\]
+	The dimension factor reflects the normalized-trace convention used for
+	finite matrix states in Lean.
+\end{definition}

+\begin{lemma}[Formalization support for marginal evaluation]
+	\label{lem:left-marginal-state-evaluation}

+	\uses{def:left-marginal-state}

+		= \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{norm}}\!\bigl(\rho_{\mathsf A}X\bigr).
+	\]
+\end{lemma}
+\begin{proof}
+	\leanok
+	Expand both normalized traces in the chosen product basis and sum the
+	diagonal $\mathsf B$-blocks.
+\end{proof}

+	\leanok

60	\begin{remark}
    61	  Unless specified otherwise, all strategies considered in this paper are tensor
    62	  product strategies, and we simply call them \emph{strategies}.
    63	  Similarly, we refer to $\val^*(\game)$ as the \emph{value} of the game
    64	  $\game$.
    65	\end{remark}
    66	
    67	
    68	\begin{definition}[Projective strategies]
    69	  \label{def:projective-strategy}
    70	  We say that a strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ is \emph{projective} if
    71	  all the measurements $\{A^x_a\}_a$ and $\{B^y_b\}_b$ are projective.
    72	\end{definition}
    73	
    74	\begin{definition}\label{rem:symmetric-games}
    75		A game $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ is
    76	  \emph{symmetric} if the question and answer alphabets are the same for both
    77	  players (i.e.\
    78	  $\cal{X} = \cal{Y}$ and $\cal{A} = \cal{B}$), the distribution $\mu$ is
    79	  symmetric (i.e.\
    80	  $\mu(x,y) = \mu(y,x)$), and the decision predicate $D$ treats both players
    81	  symmetrically (i.e.\ for all $x,y,a,b$, $D(x,y,a,b) = D(y,x,b,a)$).
    82	 
    83	We call a strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$
    84	  \emph{symmetric} if $\ket{\psi}$ is a (pure) state in $\mH \otimes \mH$, for some
    85	  Hilbert space $\mH$, that is invariant under permutation of the two factors,
    86	  and the measurement operators of both players are identical.
    87	\end{definition}
    88	
    89	We often specify symmetric games $\game$ and symmetric strategies $\strategy$ using
    90	  a compact notation: we write $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{A}, \mu, D)$ and
    91	  $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, M)$ where $M$ denotes the set of measurement
    92	  operators for both players.
    93	
    94	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:symmetric-strat}
    95	  Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{A},  \mu, D)$ be a symmetric game
    96	  such that $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$ for some $\eps\geq 0$.
    97	  Then there exists a symmetric and projective strategy
    98	  $\strategy=(\ket{\psi},M)$ such that $\val^*(\game,\strategy)\geq 1-\eps$.
    99	\end{lemma}
   100	
   101	\begin{proof}
   102	  By definition for any $\eps'>\eps$ there exists a strategy $\strategy'= (\ket{\psi'},A,B)$ such
   103	  that $\val^*(\game,\strategy')\geq 1-\eps'$.
   104	Using Naimark's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark}) we can assume
   105	without loss of generality that $\ket{\psi'}\in\C_{\alice'}^d\otimes \C_{\bob'}^d$ for some integer $d$
   106	  and that for every $x$, $A^x$ and $B^x$ are projective measurements.
   107	Let
   108	  \[
   109	    \ket{\psi} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \big( \ket{0}_\alice \ket{1}_\bob
   110	    \ket{\psi'}_{\alice'\bob'} + \ket{1}_\alice \ket{0}_\bob
   111	    \ket{\psi'_\tau}_{\alice'\bob'}\big) \in (\C_{\alice}^2 \otimes
   112	    \C_{\alice'}^d) \otimes (\C_\bob^2 \otimes \C_{\bob'}^d)\;,
   113	  \]
   114	  where $\ket{\psi'_\tau}$ is obtained from $\ket{\psi}$ by permuting the two
   115	  players' registers.
   116	  Observe that $\ket{\psi}$ is invariant under permutation of $\alice\alice'$
   117	  and $\bob\bob'$.
   118	
   119	  For any question $x\in \cal{X}$ define the measurement $M^x = \{M^x_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$
   120	  acting on the Hilbert space $\C^2 \otimes \C^d$ as follows:
   121	  \[
   122	  	M^x_a = \ketbra{0}{0} \otimes A^x_a + \ketbra{1}{1} \otimes B^x_a \;,
   123	  \]
   124		i.e.\ for $\ket{\varphi} \in \C^d$, $M^x_a(\ket{0}\ket{\varphi})=\ket{0}A^x_a\ket{\varphi}$ and $M^x_a(\ket{1}\ket{\varphi})=\ket{1}B^x_a\ket{\varphi}$.
   125	  When Alice receives question $x$, she measures $M^x$ on registers $\alice \alice'$, and when Bob receives 
   126	  question $y$, he measures $M^y$ on registers $\bob \bob'$.
   127	Using that by assumption the decision predicate $D$ for $\game$ is symmetric,
   128	  it is not hard to verify that $\val^*(\game,\strategy) =
   129	  \val^*(\game,\strategy')$.

   132	\begin{definition}
   133	  \label{def:comm-strategy}
   134	  Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ be a game, and let
   135	  $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ be a strategy for $\game$ such that  $\mH_A = \mH_B$.
   136	  Let $S \subseteq \cal{X} \times \cal{Y}$ denote the support of the question
   137	  distribution $\mu$, i.e.\ the set of $(x,y)$ such that $\mu(x,y)>0$.
   138	  We say that $\strategy$ is a \emph{commuting strategy for $\game$} if for all
   139	  question pairs $(x, y) \in S$, we have $[A^x_a, B^y_b] = 0$ 
   140	  for all $a
   141	  \in \cal{A}, b \in \cal{B}$, where $[A, B] = AB - BA$ denotes the commutator.
   142	\end{definition}

   144	\begin{definition}[Consistent measurements]
   145	  \label{def:consistent-measurement}
   146	  Let $\cal{A}$ be a finite set, let $\ket{\psi} \in \mH \otimes \mH$ be a
   147	  state, and let $\{ M_a \}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ be a projective measurement on
   148	  $\mH$.
   149	  We say that \emph{$\{M_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$} if
   150	  and only if
   151	  \begin{equation*}
   152	    \forall a \in \mA\;,\quad M_a \otimes \Id_\bob\, \ket{\psi}
   153	    = \Id_\alice \otimes M_a\, \ket{\psi}\;.
   154	  \end{equation*}
   155		When the state $\ket{\psi}$ is clear from context we simply say that \emph{$\{M_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is consistent}.
   156	\end{definition}
   157	
   158	The terminology ``consistent'' arises from the fact that when the measurement $\{M_a\}$ is performed on both registers of $\ket{\psi}$, the probability of obtaining twice the same outcome is 
   159	\[ \sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \otimes M_a \ket{\psi}\,=\, \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Id_\alice \otimes (M_a)^2 \ket{\psi} \,=\, \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Id_\alice \otimes M_a \ket{\psi} \,=\,1\;,\]
   160	where the first equality is by definition of consistency, the second uses that $\{M_a\}$ is projective, and the last uses $\sum_a M_a=\Id$. 
   161	
   162	\begin{definition}[Consistent strategies]
   163	  \label{def:consistent-strategy}
   164		Let $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ be a projective strategy with state
   165	  $\ket{\psi} \in \mH \otimes \mH$, for some Hilbert space~$\mH$, which is
   166	  defined on question alphabets $\cal{X}$ and~$\cal{Y}$ and answer alphabets
   167	  $\cal{A}$ and~$\cal{B}$, respectively.
   168	  We say that the strategy $\strategy$ is \emph{consistent} if for all $x \in
   169	  \cal{X}$, the measurement $\{A^x_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is consistent on
   170	  $\ket{\psi}$ and if for all $y \in \cal{Y}$, the measurement $\{B^y_b\}_{b \in
   171	    \cal{B}}$ is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$.
   172	\end{definition}
   173	
   174	We almost always restrict our attention to symmetric strategies. In this case, consistency implies that whenever both players are sent the same question, they provide the same answer.

   176	\begin{definition}
   177	  \label{def:spcc}
   178	  We say that a strategy $\strategy$ for a game $\game$ is \emph{PCC} if it is projective, consistent, and commuting for $\game$.
   179	  Additionally, we say that a PCC strategy $\strategy$ is \emph{SPCC} if it is furthermore symmetric.
   180	\end{definition}

   313	\begin{fact}[Fact 4.20 in~\cite{NW19}]
   314	  \label{fact:add-a-proj}
   315	  Let $\cal{A},\cal{B},\cal{C}$ be finite sets, and let $\mu$ be a distribution
   316	  over question pairs $(x,y)$.
   317	  Let $\{A_{a,b}^x\}$ and $\{B_{a,b}^x\}$ be operators whose outcomes range over the
   318	  product set $\cal{A} \times \cal{B}$.
   319	  Suppose a set of operators $\{C_{a,c}^y\}$, whose outcomes range over the
   320	  product set $\cal{A} \times \cal{C}$, satisfies the condition $\sum_{c}
   321	  (C_{a,c}^y)^\dagger C_{a,c}^y \leq \Id$ for all $a$ and all $y$.
   322	  If $A_{a,b}^x \approx_\delta B_{a,b}^x$ on average over $x$ sampled from the
   323	  corresponding marginal of distribution $\mu$, then $C^y_{a,c} A^x_{a,b}
   324	  \approx_\delta C^y_{a,c} B^x_{a,b}$ on average over $(x,y)$ sampled from $\mu$.
   325	\end{fact}
   326	\begin{proof}
   327	  Fix questions $x,y$ and answers $a \in \cal{A},b \in \cal{B}$. We have then that
   328	  \begin{align}
   329	    \sum_{c} \left \| (C^y_{a,c} A^x_{a,b} - C^y_{a,c} B^x_{a,b} ) \ket{\psi} \right \|^2
   330	    & = \sum_{c} \bra{\psi} (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b})^\dagger (C^y_{a,c})^\dagger (C^y_{a,c})
   331	      (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b} ) \ket{\psi}\\
   332	    & \leq \bra{\psi} (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b})^\dagger
   333	      (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b} ) \ket{\psi} \\
   334	    & = \left \| (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b})\ket{\psi} \right \|^2
   335	  \end{align}
   336	  where the inequality follows from the assumption that $\sum_c (C_{a,c}^y)^\dagger
   337	  C_{a,c}^y \leq \Id$.
   338	  Thus we obtain the desired conclusion
   339	  \begin{equation*}
   340	    \E_{(x,y) \sim \mu} \sum_{a,b,c} \left \| (C^y_{a,c} A^x_{a,b} - C^y_{a,c} B^x_{a,b} )
   341	      \ket{\psi} \right \|^2 	\leq \E_{(x,y) \sim \mu} \sum_{a,b}
   342	    \left \| (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b})\ket{\psi} \right \|^2 \leq \delta.
   343	  \end{equation*}
   344	\end{proof}

   347	\begin{fact}
   348	\label{fact:add-a-proj2}
   349	Let $\mathcal{X},\mathcal{A}$ denote finite sets, and let $\mathcal{G}$ denote a set of functions $g: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{A}$. Let $\{A^x_a \}$, $\{B^x_a\}$ be POVMs indexed by $\mathcal{X}$ and outcomes in $\mathcal{A}$. Let $\{ S_g^x \}_{x\in \mathcal{X}, g\in\mathcal{G}}$ denote a set of operators such that for all $x \in \mathcal{X}$, $\sum_g (S_g^x)^\dagger S_g^x \leq \Id$. 
   350	If $A^x_a \approx_\delta B^x_a$ on average over $x$, then $S_g^x A^x_{g(x)} \approx_\delta S_g^x B^x_{g(x)}$. 
   351	\end{fact}
   352	\begin{proof}
   353		We expand:
   354		\begin{align*}
   355			\E_x \sum_g \norm{ S^x_g (A^x_{g(x)} - B^x_{g(x)}) \ket{\psi}}^2 &= \E_x \sum_g \bra{\psi} (A^x_{g(x)} - B^x_{g(x)})^\dagger  (S_g^x)^\dagger S_g^x (A^x_{g(x)} - B^x_{g(x)}) \ket{\psi} \\
   356			&= \E_x \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A^x_a - B^x_a)^\dagger  \Big(\sum_{g: g(x) = a} (S_g^x)^\dagger S_g^x \Big) (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi} \\
   357			&\leq \E_x \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A^x_a - B^x_a)^\dagger (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi} \\
   358			&= \E_x \sum_a \norm{ (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi} }^2.
   359		\end{align*}
   360		The inequality follows from the fact that $\sum_{g: g(x) = a} (S_g^x)^\dagger S_g^x \leq \sum_g (S_g^x)^\dagger (S_g^x) \leq \Id$. The last line is at most $\delta$ by assumption, and we obtain the desired conclusion.
   361	\end{proof}

   364	\begin{lemma}
   365	\label{lem:cool-closeness-fact}
   366	Let $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{A}$ be finite sets and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mX$. Let $\{A^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}$ be a projective measurement and let $\{B^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}$ be a set of matrices. If $A^x_a \approx_\delta B^x_a$, then for all subsets $S \subseteq \mathcal{A}$, we have
   367	\[
   368		\sum_{a \in S} A^x_a \approx_\delta \sum_{a \in S} A^x_a \cdot B^x_a.
   369	\]
   370	\end{lemma}
   371	\begin{proof}
   372	We expand:
   373	\begin{align*}
   374		\E_x \norm{ \sum_{a \in S} \Big(A^x_a - A^x_a \cdot B^x_a\Big) \ket{\psi}}^2 &= \E_x \norm{ \sum_{a \in S} A^x_a \cdot \Big(A^x_a - B^x_a\Big) \ket{\psi}}^2 \\
   375		&= \E_x \sum_{a \in S} \bra{\psi} (A^x_a - B^x_a)^\dagger A^x_a (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi} \\
   376		&\leq \E_x \sum_a \norm{ (A^x_a -  B^x_a) \ket{\psi}}^2\;,
   377	\end{align*}
   378	where all expectations are taken according to $\mu$. 
   379	In the second line we used the projectivity of $\{ A^x_a \}$, and in the third line we used that $A^x_a \leq \Id$.
   380	\end{proof}

   404	The state-dependent distance is the right tool for reasoning about the closeness
   405	of measurement operators in a strategy.
   406	The following lemma ensures that, when two families of measurements are close on a
   407	state, changing from one family of measurement to the other only introduces
   408	a small error to the value of the strategy.
   409	
   410	\begin{lemma}
   411	  \label{lem:commutation-analysis}
   412	  Let $\{A^x_{a,\, b}\}$, $\{B^x_{a,\, b,\, c}\}$, $\{C^x_{a,\, c}\}$ be POVMs.
   413	  Suppose $\{B^x_{a,\, b,\, c}\}$ is projective, and
   414	  \begin{align*}
   415	    A^x_{a,\, b} \otimes \Id_\bob &\approx_\delta \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, b}\;,\\
   416	    C^x_{a,\, c} \otimes \Id_\bob &\approx_\delta \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, c}\;,
   417	  \end{align*}
   418		where recall that $B^x_{a,\, b} = \sum_c B^x_{a,b,c}$ and similarly $B^x_{a,\, c}=\sum_b B^x_{a,b,c}$. 
   419	  Then the following approximate commutation relation holds:
   420	  \begin{equation*}
   421	    [A^x_{a,\, b}, C^x_{a,\, c}] \otimes I_\bob \approx_\delta 0\;.
   422	  \end{equation*}
   423	\end{lemma}
   424	
   425	\begin{proof}
   426	  Applying Fact~\ref{fact:add-a-proj} to $C^x_{a,\, c} \otimes \Id_\bob
   427	  \approx_\delta \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, c}$ and $\{A^x_{a,b} \otimes
   428	  \Id_\bob \}$, we have
   429	  \begin{equation}
   430	    \label{eq:commutation-analysis-1}
   431	    A^x_{a,\, b} C^x_{a,\, c} \otimes \Id_\bob
   432	    \approx_\delta A^x_{a,\, b} \otimes B^x_{a,\, c}\,.
   433	  \end{equation}
   434	  Similarly, applying Fact~\ref{fact:add-a-proj} to $A^x_{a,\, b} \otimes
   435	  \Id_\bob \approx_\delta \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, b}$ and $\{\Id_\alice
   436	  \otimes B^x_{a,c}\}$, and using the fact that $\{B^x_{a,b,c}\}$ is projective,
   437	  we have
   438	  \begin{equation}
   439	    \label{eq:commutation-analysis-2}
   440	    \begin{split}
   441	      A^x_{a,\, b} \otimes B^x_{a,\, c}
   442	      & \approx_\delta \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, c} B^x_{a,\, b}\\
   443	      & =_{\phantom{\delta}} \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, b,\, c}\,.
   444	    \end{split}
   445	  \end{equation}
   446	  Combining Equations~\eqref{eq:commutation-analysis-1}
   447	  and~\eqref{eq:commutation-analysis-2}, we have
   448	  \begin{equation}
   449	    \label{eq:commutation-analysis-3}
   450	    A^x_{a,\, b} C^x_{a,\, c} \otimes \Id_\bob \approx_\delta
   451	    \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, b,\, c}\,.
   452	  \end{equation}
   453	  A similar argument gives
   454	  \begin{equation}
   455	    \label{eq:commutation-analysis-4}
   456	    C^x_{a,\, c} A^x_{a,\, b} \otimes \Id_\bob \approx_\delta
   457	    \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, b,\, c}\,.
   458	  \end{equation}
   459	  The claim follows from Equations~\eqref{eq:commutation-analysis-3}
   460	  and~\eqref{eq:commutation-analysis-4}.
   461	\end{proof}

### Additional rules:
- **Section names in Lean**: use mathematical terms (`section QuantumSoundness`, `section SelfImprovement`, `section PastingLemma`), not organizational terms (`section Assembly`, `section Pipeline`).
- **Internal LaTeX labels** (e.g., `\label{ch:soundness}`) are not reader-facing and need not be renamed if doing so would break cross-references. But NEW labels should follow the standard.
- **Definitions that are actually theorems**: if a statement asserts a mathematical fact, it must be `\begin{theorem}`, not `\begin{definition}`. Definitions introduce new objects; theorems prove properties.

## `\uses` Dependency Guidelines
- **Statement `\uses`**: list only what's needed to *state* the result (typically definitions of the objects involved). Keep minimal — transitive deps are automatic.
- **Proof `\uses`**: list only what the proof *actually calls*. Don't list definitions unless the proof unfolds that definition.
- **Never self-reference**: a proof's `\uses` must NOT include the label of the theorem it proves.

## Recording Formalization-Only Lemmas
Some Lean lemmas are genuine proof infrastructure rather than named statements
from the original papers. These must be traceable without making the blueprint
look as if the paper stated them.

- If a declaration directly formalizes a paper or blueprint statement, record
  it as usual with `\lean{...}` on that statement and cite the relevant source.
- If a public declaration is an auxiliary lemma introduced only for the Lean
  proof, make that status explicit. Its Lean docstring should say that it is a
  formalization-only auxiliary lemma and should name the nearby paper equation,
  line range, or blueprint result it supports.
- If such an auxiliary declaration is important enough to be referenced from
  the blueprint, give it a clearly subordinate blueprint node, for example
  `[Formalization support for ...]`, and state in the first sentence that the
  lemma is not a named statement of the paper but isolates a step used in the
  Lean proof.
- Connect auxiliary nodes to the corresponding result from the paper with `\uses{...}` from
  the proof that actually calls them. Do not add them only to silence a sync
  warning; the dependency edge should explain where the auxiliary result is
  used.
- Do not mark an auxiliary node with proof-level `\leanok` unless its Lean proof
  is complete and `#print axioms` has no `sorryAx`. Statement-level `\leanok`
  is acceptable only when the Lean statement is intentionally recorded but the
  proof remains tracked as incomplete.

## Blueprint Structure
- `content.tex` is a router: `\input{chapter/ch01_intro}` etc.
- Each chapter is a separate file in `chapter/`
- Definitions/theorems numbered within chapters: `\newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}[chapter]`

## Lean Blueprint Macros
- `\lean{Namespace.DeclName}` — links to Lean declaration
- `\leanok` — context-sensitive marker; see "Statement-level vs proof-level `\leanok`" below
- `\uses{label1, label2}` — declares dependency edges for the graph
- `\notready` — marks as not ready for formalization (orange in graph)
- `\mathlibok` — already in Mathlib (dark green in graph; see legend note below)

### Statement-level vs proof-level `\leanok`

`\leanok` is context-sensitive for human review and graph interpretation. The same macro is used for two different claims, so reviewers should read it by placement rather than by raw token count.

**Statement-level `\leanok`.** Place this inside a `theorem`, `lemma`, `proposition`, `corollary`, or `definition` environment, on its own line immediately after `\lean{...}`. It says that the corresponding Lean declaration exists and that its statement matches the blueprint or paper statement. It does **not** say that the Lean proof already exists or is complete. For definitions, this is the only `\leanok` marker.

**Proof-level `\leanok`.** Place this inside the matching `proof` environment, preferably as the first line after `\begin{proof}`. The canonical current placement is the theorem `thm:commutativity-points` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch08_commutativity.tex:8-19`, where the statement block has `\leanok` immediately after `\lean{...}` and the proof block begins with another `\leanok`. This marker says that the Lean proof is complete and free of unresolved `sorry` or unjustified project-level `axiom` shortcuts. In particular, `#print axioms <decl>` must show no `sorryAx`, and the declaration must satisfy the broader blocker rules in the lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference and [`docs/project_conventions.md`](project_conventions.md).

A theorem, lemma, proposition, or corollary node is **fully formalized in Lean if and only if it has both markers**: statement-level `\leanok` in the statement block and proof-level `\leanok` in the proof block. Statement-level without proof-level means “the statement has been transcribed and matched, but the proof is not yet certified complete.” Definitions have no proof block, so statement-level `\leanok` alone is enough there.

Excerpt from `blueprint/src/chapter/ch08_commutativity.tex:8-19`:

```latex
\begin{theorem}[Commutativity of the point measurements]\label{thm:commutativity-points}
  \lean{MIPStarRE.LDT.CommutativityPoints.commutativityPoints}
  \leanok
  \uses{def:good-strategy, def:approx_delta}
  Let $(\psi,A,B,L)$ be an $(\eps,\delta,\gamma)$-good symmetric strategy.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
  \leanok
  The strategy passes the diagonal lines test with probability $1-\gamma$.
\end{proof}
```

**Current CI behavior.** The advisory Blueprint ↔ Lean sync check in [`docs/ci-blueprint-sync.md`](ci-blueprint-sync.md) distinguishes the two placements. Only proof-level `\leanok` whose axiom closure contains `sorryAx` (or whose harness output cannot be parsed) is reported as an **error**. Statement-level-only `\leanok` with the same finding is downgraded to a **warning**, because statement-level does not claim proof completeness. Each audit line is annotated with the observed placement so reviewers can tell statement-sync work apart from proof-completion work.

`leanblueprint` does not use distinct macro names for these two claims, so audits must distinguish them by environment context rather than by raw `\leanok` counts. A future split such as `\leanokstmt` / `\leanokproof` could make that distinction explicit, but that is only a possible later cleanup; the current convention is to keep `\leanok` and rely on placement.

A recurring historical example is the chapter 4 `Q/X/\widehat X/P` witness
layer.  Once Lean has construction theorems deriving the displayed identities
and estimates from the rank-reduction, sigma-range, positive-Gram, native
spectral-theorem, or rectangular-SVD hypotheses, the corresponding blueprint
entries may carry `\leanok`.  A declaration that merely projects an identity
from an opaque data record is not enough by itself, and a theorem depending on
extra rectangular-SVD data should not be used as evidence for an unconditional
paper statement unless a separate construction supplies that data.

## Dependency Graph Colors (web)
- **Light green box**: definition with `\lean` + `\leanok` (defined in Lean)
- **Green**: theorem/lemma/proposition/corollary with `\lean` + statement-level `\leanok` (statement matched in Lean)
- **Dark green**: either (i) theorem/lemma/proposition/corollary with both statement-level and proof-level `\leanok` (fully formalized in Lean), or (ii) a `\mathlibok` node
- **Blue**: ready to state/prove (all deps are done)
- **Orange**: `\notready` (needs more blueprint work)

## Bibliography Workflow
1. Edit `blueprint/src/references.bib` (standalone, AuthorYYYYKeyword keys)
2. Run `texra-blueprint bbl` from the repository root — it regenerates
   `blueprint/src/web.bbl` from the `\cite` keys in the blueprint sources.
   `web.bbl` is not committed (`.gitignore` covers `*.bbl`); every CI job
   that runs the web build regenerates it first, and so must a local run.
3. Run `leanblueprint web` (plasTeX reads `web.bbl`)
4. The PDF build needs no separate step: `leanblueprint pdf` runs bibtex on
   `print.tex` itself, and `print.bbl` never feeds the web build.
5. Citation key format: e.g., `Ji2020MIPStar`, `Natarajan2020Quantum`
6. Paper-gap notes: blueprint prose cites `\cite{gap:<slug>}` (never the raw
   `docs/paper-gaps/<slug>.tex` path); each cited note has a `@techreport`
   entry in `blueprint/src/references.bib` with `type = {Paper-gap note}`,
   whose `note` field carries the published PDF URL as `\url{...}` (the
   alpha style of the PDF build drops `url` fields for techreport entries).
   `texra-blueprint bbl` renders such entries with slug-shaped citation
   labels (e.g. `[issue-906-main-formal-k-bound]`) in the web bibliography,
   while ordinary entries keep alpha labels. Lean docstrings and comments
   keep the repository path form.
